stops.name: Slankamen, the mounting mountain of debt
stops.campa: At Slankamen on the Danube, Ludwig of Baden smashes the Ottoman army in one of the bloodiest fields of the age, and the victory, like all the others, is fed from Samuel's stores. But the ledger tells a second story beneath the triumph. The crown's debt to him swells from 187,000 gulden in 1684 toward the millions: he advances endlessly to a treasury that pays him in privileges, promises, and suspicion. He charges his twelve per cent, his commissions, his exchange fees, and still the arrears outrun them.

stops.name: Zenta, the debt at three million as Eugene triumphs
stops.campa: At Zenta on the Tisza, Prince Eugene of Savoy falls upon the Ottoman army mid-crossing and annihilates it: the victory that will force the Turk to Karlowitz. Eugene's armies march on Oppenheimer's provisions; it is the Oberfaktor who arranges even their field hospitals and medicine. Yet as the greatest of imperial victories is won on his supply, the crown's debt to him has climbed past three million florins, and the treasury under his enemies plots how never to pay it. Triumph abroad, strangulation at home: the two halves of his life meet on this field.

stops.name: Vienna, Bishop Kollonitsch and the fabricated murder
stops.campa: Bishop Leopold Kollonitsch, raised to head the imperial treasury, sets himself to break the court's dependence on the Jew. He levels a charge as monstrous as it is groundless: that Samuel has plotted the murder of his own kinsman and cashier, Samson Wertheimer. Oppenheimer and his household are arrested and cast into prison as defrauders of the state. The accusation is a court intrigue dressed as a crime: the enemies within striking at the man the enemies without could not.

stops.name: Vienna, ransomed from prison
stops.campa: The investigation proves the charges empty, but the crown does not free him for justice's sake. He buys his own liberty: 500,000 florins to the treasury, and a fresh half-million in credit besides, before the doors open. He walks out poorer and more indispensable than ever, the debt owed to him now standing near three million florins. The lesson is bitter and plain: to serve the Caesar is to be squeezed by him, and to be needed is no shield at all.

stops.name: Vienna, Rossau: the cemetery wall and the hospital
stops.campa: Restored to favour, Samuel turns his wealth to his people. In the Rossau, along the Seegasse, he buys the old burial ground and rebuilds in stone the wall the Turks tore down in the siege of 1683. Two years on he raises beside it the first Jewish hospital and a house of care for the poor. Across the Reich he is a benefactor without precedent, endowing synagogues and yeshivot from his war-profits: the Oberfaktor building, quietly, a Jewish world in the city that had cast the Jews out.

stops.name: Karlowitz, the peace that starves the profit
stops.campa: At Karlowitz the long Turkish war ends; the Ottoman yields Hungary and Transylvania to the Kaiser. For the Oberfaktor peace is a double edge. The great flow of war-contracts slows, yet the crown's debt to him remains: colossal, unpaid, and now harder than ever to collect from a treasury no longer terrified into borrowing. The disbanded, unpaid soldiers and invalids of the war look for someone to blame, and the richest Jew in Vienna, in his palace by the Bauernmarkt, is easy to find.

stops.name: Vienna, Bauernmarkt: the mob sacks the house
stops.campa: It begins small and turns to fury. Two chimney-sweep apprentices at play outside the tavern are mocked from Oppenheimer's house; they answer with the old Jew-baiting gesture, rapping their knuckles on a bench. When Samuel calls the watch, a crowd gathers, stones and eggs fly, and the mob storms the palace, ransacking, wrecking, hurling the great ledgers of the empire's war into the street. The household flees to a cellar vault. The city guard stands idle; only the castle guard fires at last into the crowd, killing and wounding twelve.

stops.name: Vienna, Petersplatz: the cannon and the gallows
stops.campa: That night the authorities wheel cannon onto the Petersplatz to overawe the city and prevent another rising. At dawn the ringleaders, a chimney-sweep and a sword-polisher, are hanged from the iron grating above the door of the very house they plundered, a warning left swinging over the wreck. Those who carried off the emperor's documents are promised amnesty if they return them swiftly, for the crown needs its ledgers back as badly as the Oberfaktor does. Order is restored; the man is not.

stops.name: Vienna, chief war factor for a new war
stops.campa: The War of the Spanish Succession opens, and the aged Oberfaktor is drawn back to the yoke, raised now to chief war factor, he and his two sons running the commissariat of the imperial armies across many fronts at once. His agents even shift the subsidy of half a million florins that buys the Saxon elector the crown of Poland. Old, plundered, owed millions, distrusted by the court he keeps solvent, he is still the one hand that can conjure an army's bread out of nothing.

stops.name: Vienna, death of the Oberfaktor
stops.campa: On 3 May 1703, in the city he had fed through siege and war, Samuel Oppenheimer dies at seventy-two: the most important creditor the Habsburg state has ever had, the crown owing him millions it never means to pay. He is carried to the Rossau, to the burial ground he himself walled in stone, and laid among his people in the Seegasse. The single indispensable Jew is gone; and the empire he propped up on his own credit feels the ground shift beneath it.

stops.name: Vienna, the Oppenheimer bankruptcy
stops.campa: The crown seizes its escape. Rather than honour its debt, the state refuses the heir Emanuel his six million florins, declares the firm bankrupt, and turns the accusation round, demanding four million from him instead, on the ancient pretext that the fortune was fraud from the start. The whole edifice of personal credit, built on trust alone, buckles at once; the exchanges linked to Oppenheimer, above all Frankfurt, plunge into crisis. His death nearly drags the empire down with it.

stops.name: Vienna, the Banco del Giro rises from the ruin
stops.campa: To catch a state falling through the hole one man's death has torn, Austria founds in 1703 its first public bank, the Banco del Giro. Where credit had rested on the trust of a single household, it must now rest on an institution. The Oberfaktor's method is nationalised over his open grave: the personal genius of the Court Jew becomes the impersonal machinery of state finance: the very thing that will make men like him, in time, no longer indispensable.
